references.title: Artist Talk - Grégory Chatonsky: INFRALLUCINATION
references.description: French-Canadian artist Grégory Chatonsky, a pioneer of net art and among the first artists to work through machine learning presents a lecture titled "INFRALLUCINATION."Hallucination has become the ambivalent concept of our digital era: oscillating between an error to be corrected and a driver of radical inventiveness. Far from abstract theories, this conference proposes approaching artificial hallucination through the lens of artistic experience. Gregory Chatonsky explores how AI redefines our relationship with reality and memory. Through a journey across his works, he questions: how does a machine hallucinate? How does this "ontological pareidolia" transform our own imagination? A reflection on a machine that, through its signs, becomes the language-based hallucination of the world. Free and open to the public.RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Related programming: Exhibition: Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and HallucinationsExhibition Dates: September 3 - October 3, 2026 Opening Reception: Thursday, September 3, 4-6:30pm, Worth Ryder Art GalleryArtist Talk, Gregory Chatonsky "INFRALLUCINATION": Thursday, September 3, 6:30-8:00pm, AAPB 285Film Program, Push Buttons and AI (https://bampfa.org/event/push-buttons-and-ai): September 9, 7 pm, BAMPFACuratorial Tour, led by Antonio Somaini: Friday, September 11, 4:30pm, Worth Ryder Art GalleryWorkshop on Latent Space of Culture: September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days, 470 StephensSalon on AI and Art: September 16, 6pm– 9pm, AI Futures LabTour of AI: October 3 Reservations required. references.title: Empowered by AI: Create a More Breathable, Sustainable Workday (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
references.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) Higher education staff are navigating unprecedented workload pressures: increasing demands, shrinking resources, and the nonstop expectation to do more with less. Meanwhile, AI has entered the workplace—but most employees are unsure how to use it effectively, ethically, or in ways that genuinely reduce overwhelm rather than add to it. This session reframes AI through a human-centered, wellness-first lens. Instead of treating AI as a productivity mandate, participants will learn how to use AI as a tool for clarity, boundaries, and sustainable success. Using Helanah Warren's "Breathable Workday Framework," this interactive workshop demonstrates how AI can help UC staff reclaim time, reduce cognitive load, and create more space for the work that matters—without burnout, tech fatigue, or over-automation.Learning Outcomes: –How to use AI to streamline tasks like email, communication, planning, and documentation. –Scripts, prompts, and workflows that turn overwhelm into clarity. –Micro-boundaries that prevent AI from becoming "one more thing." –A 3-step model for integrating AI ethically and sustainably. –Somatic and mindset strategies to stay grounded during tech-driven change.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as the virtual workshop date draws near.

references.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market"
references.description: Abstract: We use advances in natural language processing to construct new measures of workers' tasklevel exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning from 2010 to 2023, capturing variation across firms, occupations, and time. Tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently experience reduced labor demand. To interpret these patterns, we develop a model that separates direct substitution from indirect reallocative effects of labor-saving technologies. Two variables summarize the impact of AI on within-firm labor demand: the mean exposure of an occupation's tasks, which depresses demand, and the concentration of exposure in a few tasks, which offsets losses by enabling workers to reallocate effort. Using an instrument based on historical university hiring networks, we find causal evidence consistent with these predictions. Despite strong substitution at the task level, overall employment effects are modest, as reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.

references.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Mathew Hauer and Tyler McCormick: "AI in Demography"
references.description: Mathew E. Hauer is the Charles B. Nam Associate Professor of Sociology at Florida State University, Assistant Director of the Center for Demography and Population Health, and the Head of AI Agent Development at Aaru, a company focused on artificial intelligence and simulation (https://aaru.com/). His research lies at the intersection of demography, migration, population projections, and climate change, with particular expertise in modeling future population dynamics under climate stress. His work on climate migration and population vulnerability has earned numerous prestigious accolades, including the 2024 Early Achievement Award (https://www.populationassociation.org/about/annual-awards/early-achievement-award#:~:text=The%20Early%20Achievement%20award%20recognizes,scholars%20who%20received%20their%20Ph.) from the Population Association of America and the 2023 Cozzarelli Prize (http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/pnas-cozzarelli-2022.html) from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, and is a finalist for the 2025 Cozzarelli Prize and the Max Planck-Humboldt Research Award. He is a two-time recipient of the E. Walter Terrie Award (https://www.sda-demography.org/Terrie-Award) for excellence in applied demography, and his dissertation on sea-level rise and human migration has accumulated over 1,500 citations since 2016. Dr. Hauer's research has significantly shaped our understanding of climate change's demographic impacts, from sea-level rise displacement to temperature extremes and coastal flooding. His work has been featured in over 800 media outlets worldwide, including the New York Times, The Guardian, Time Magazine, National Geographic, and the Washington Post. Before joining FSU, he spent nearly a decade directing the Applied Demography Program at the University of Georgia. Tyler McCormick's work develops statistical models for inference and prediction in scientific settings where data are sparsely observed or measured with error, with a particular focus on measuring and understanding human behavior. His recent projects include estimating features of social networks (e.g. the degree of clustering or how central an individual is) using data from standard surveys, inferring a likely cause of death (when deaths happen outside of hospitals) using reports from surviving caretakers, and quantifying & communicating uncertainty in predictive models for global health policymakers. He holds a Ph.D. in Statistics (with distinction) from Columbia University and is the recipient of the NIH Director's New Innovator Award, NIH Career Development (K01) Award, Army Research Office Young Investigator Program Award, and a Google Faculty Research Award. Currently, he is a Professor of Statistics and Sociology at the University of Washington, where he is also a core faculty member in the Center for Statistics and the Social Sciences and a Senior Data Science Fellow at the eScience Institute. During the 2019-2020 academic year Tyler was a Visiting Faculty Researcher at Google People+AI Research (PAIR). Tyler is the former Editor of the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics (JCGS) and a Fellow of the American Statistical Association. Tyler is currently a member of the Committee on Applied and Theoretical Statistics at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, & Medicine. More information on Tyler's work is here: https://thmccormick.github.io (https://thmccormick.github.io/).

references.title: Film Screening: Push Buttons and AI
references.description: In conjunction with the exhibition Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations at UC Berkeley's Worth Ryder Gallery, Antonio Somaini, Hannes Bajohr, and Sonja Thiel present a program of works about AI and its social and technical infrastructures. Gibbs Chapman's Push Button is a dryly funny exposé of the effects of automation on twenty-first-century humans, while Inès Sieulle's The Oasis I Deserve documents affective interactions with the chatbot Replika. Nicolas Gourault reveals the numbing human labor that feeds AI with Their Eyes, while the studio Taller Estampa uses classic film clips to demonstrate how the object recognition software YOLO9000 sees and classifies. AI eats itself and ends in "model collapse" in Egor Kraft's One & Infinite Chairs. references.title: Workshop: The Latent Spaces of Culture
references.description: Latent spaces are a foundational concept in contemporary artificial intelligence. They enable complex data—images, texts, sounds, and other digital objects—to be represented as high-dimensional structures in which relationships, patterns, and similarities can be modeled computationally. By translating intricate datasets into compressed mathematical representations, latent spaces allow AI systems not only to analyze information but also to generate new content; often, this content is itself cultural in nature. Yet the cultural and epistemological implications of latent spaces remain comparatively underexplored, particularly their role in shaping creativity, cultural memory, and representation. This three-day workshop, part of the France–Berkeley Fund project "The Latent Spaces of Culture," brings together researchers from UC Berkeley and institutions in France to examine these questions and explore latent space as both a technical architecture and a cultural form. (September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days)https://german.berkeley.edu/latent-spaces-culture (https://german.berkeley.edu/latent-spaces-culture)

references.title: CSLS Speaker Series: "The Distribution of Federally-Insured Mortgages: 1935-1975, Evidence from Local Land Records"
references.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
references.description: featuring Omer Ali, Assistant Professor of Economics, University of PittsburghAbstract: This project develops a novel dataset of federally-insured mortgages from 1935 to 1975 by digitizing local land records from county recorders of deeds across a geographically diverse set of U.S. counties. Despite the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and Veterans Administration (VA) programs accounting for up to 50% of all mortgages for some years during this period, systematic borrower-level data has been unavailable due to a lack of federal records and decentralized county recording systems. Using a new pipeline that deploys large language models to digitize scanned mortgages, we identify and extract information from FHA-insured and VA-guaranteed mortgages, geolocate properties, and link borrowers to full-count Census data from 1940 and 1950. This produces the first comprehensive address- and borrower-level dataset beyond 1940. We investigate the share of Black borrowers among FHA and VA mortgage recipients, characterize the spatial distribution of mortgages across neighborhoods that vary in racial composition and HOLC ratings, and examine the demographic and socioeconomic characteristics of borrowers. The analysis enhances our understanding of how federal housing policy shaped metropolitan development and racial inequality during the New Deal and Civil Rights eras. (Joint with Jacob Faber, Andreas Ferrara, Jonathan Rose, Thomas Storrs, Katherine Thomas, Gabrielle Toborg, Randall Walsh, and Wenfei Xu)

references.title: Dissertation Talk: Verifying Secure Execution for Systems with Untrusted Components
references.description: The question of trust lies at the center of modern systems: they rely on complex components that may be compromised by an adversary. Even when one component cannot be trusted, trust in the system's behavior naturally falls apart. Techniques that enable verification of expected behavior address this challenge. To this end, we introduce new techniques for efficiently verifying secure execution across a variety of systems, from cryptographic systems to AI agents. First, we present Whisper, a system for large-scale private telemetry in the two-server setting that achieves orders of magnitude reduction in server-to-server communication when verifying that measurements are individually well-formed. After that, we look at the problem of verifiable private information retrieval, where a client privately fetches information from a remote server while verifying that the server does not cheat. We present a new protocol that reduces the client's storage by orders of magnitude for standard database sizes and a deployment mode to practically bring this technology to millions of devices. Towards the end, we transition to the world of AI agents. We present Pincer, a system that augments agents with a digital twin that verifies their actions against automatically learned user preferences.

references.title: Josette Melchor // Newtemporary: Designing in the Space Between New and Next
references.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Josette Melchor, founder and cultural strategist working across art, technology, cities, and responsible AI. As the founder of Gray Area and now Newtemporary — and a board member of the Burning Man Project — Josette has spent her career shaping experiences that connect emerging technologies with civic life, cultural infrastructure, and public imagination. Her work moves fluidly across spatial strategy, immersive media, curation, and systems thinking, always with an eye toward how culture and technology evolve together. ​In this talk, Josette will explore the idea behind Newtemporary, the notion that everything from culture to place to technology is always in transition. references.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten: Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization
references.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization Abstract Classical hypothesis testing frameworks break down in contemporary settings in which null hypotheses are increasingly abstract, the same data are used to both generate and test hypotheses, and minimal assumptions about the underlying data are made. In this work, we propose a new framework for conducting valid hypothesis tests in broad contexts. We propose to add and subtract external noise generated from a symmetric shift-family to our data, X, to partition it into two pieces, X1 and X2. We provide a generic strategy for orthogonalizing X2 against X1 under the null hypothesis H0, then show that testing whether the orthogonalization was successful provides a valid test of H0 under mild assumptions. Remarkably, this framework extends naturally to the post-selection inference setting with minimal modifications: we simply select a hypothesis on X1, then perform orthogonalization under the selected null. As our approach neither requires pre-specification of the selection mechanism, nor is restricted to a small class of data-generating distributions, it dramatically expands the settings for which valid post-selection inference can be conducted. We showcase the flexibility of our proposal in a number of case studies. This is joint work with Ameer Dharamshi (McGill University) and Runjia Zou (University of Washington). Bio Daniela Witten is a professor of Statistics and Biostatistics at University of Washington, and the Dorothy Gilford Endowed Chair in Mathematical Statistics. She develops statistical machine learning methods for high-dimensional data, with a focus on unsupervised learning. She has received a number of awards for her research in statistical machine learning: most notably the Spiegelman Award from the American Public Health Association for a (bio)statistician under age 40, and the Presidents' Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies for a statistician under age 41. Daniela is a co-author of the textbook "Introduction to Statistical Learning", and has served as Joint Editor of Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B. references.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy: Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting
references.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting Abstract We present our ongoing work on the development of an online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that personalizes delivery of interventions sequentially, over time, to members of a dyad. The RL algorithm is one component in the design of the digital health intervention. Different RL components target different elements of the dyad; these elements are a target individual, a carepartner and their relationship. The RL algorithm is a multi-agent RL algorithm in which the 3 agents make decisions on the 3 elements of the dyad. We incorporate domain knowledge in the form of approximal causal directed acyclic graphs to speed up online learning in this sparse data setting. This work is motivated by our development of the ADAPTS-HCT multi-agent RL algorithm, designed to improve medication adherence by young adults who have undergone a blood and bone marrow transplant. The RL algorithm will be deployed in a clinical trial in late summer 2026. BioSusan A. Murphy is Mallinckrodt Professor of Statistics and of Computer Science and Associate Faculty at the Kempner Institute, Harvard University. Her research focuses on improving sequential decision making via the development of online, real-time reinforcement learning algorithms. Her lab is involved in multiple deployments of these algorithms in digital health. She is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences and of the US National Academy of Medicine. In 2013 she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for her work on experimental designs to inform sequential decision making. She is a Fellow of the College on Problems in Drug Dependence, Past-President of Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Past-President of the Bernoulli Society and a former editor of the Annals of Statistics. references.title: Architecting Human Power in the Age of AI (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
references.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) In a workplace increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, many professional development sessions focus on what tools to learn next. This session takes a different approach. It focuses on what AI cannot replace: the distinctly human ability to decide what matters, what you stand for, and how you choose to show up. This is not an AI skills workshop. It is an invitation to become more intentional about your human advantage. As AI expands what is possible, our opportunity is not to compete with technology, but to become clearer about what makes us uniquely valuable and then use AI to amplify it. By knowing what deserves your attention, what guides your decisions, and how you want to show up, you can engage AI with greater clarity and intention rather than simply using it to do more, faster. Led by Executive Coach and former Fortune 500 Marketing Leader Sarah Peterson, this interactive 90-minute session combines provocative ideas, personal reflection, and practical application. Drawing on her own journey from high-achieving executive through burnout and realignment, Sarah introduces her Leadership DNA Pyramid, a framework inspired by the strategy used to build iconic brands and adapted to help individuals navigate change, complexity, and an increasingly AI-enabled workplace. Participants will work with three dimensions of the broader Leadership DNA framework that become increasingly important as AI accelerates how we work: Priority, Value, and Presence. They will make three intentional choices: one priority to focus their energy, one value to guide their decisions, and one quality of presence to embody in how they work and lead. They will then move from insight to implementation by identifying the behaviors and actions that will bring those choices to life over the next 90 days. Together, these choices create a personal compass for working and leading with greater clarity and intention in an AI-enabled world.Learning Outcomes: –Recognize their distinctly human contribution as a source of advantage in an AI-enabled workplace. –Define one priority that deserves their focus and energy over the next 90 days. –Identify one value to intentionally guide their choices and decisions. –Choose one quality ofpresence they want to embody in how they lead, collaborate, and contribute. –Turn Priority, Value, and Presence into Practice by defining concrete behaviors and actions they can begin applying immediately.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as this virtual workshop date draws near.

references.title: AI & Disability: A Roundtable Discussion feat. Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes
references.description: A History & Theory of New Media event with Jeff Nagy, Assistant Professor, Communication and Media Studies, York University; Renée Cummings, Professor of Practice, School of Data Science, University of Virginia, and Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director, AI Equity Lab, Brookings Institution; and Os Keyes, Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Massachusetts, Lowell - Monday, September 28, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (http://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdsmOw4XW_mhfHzcHEg012STGGi9YE_lwF5AYv-7wTx4xVmJg/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=NzBtNDI4MWUzNzcwOXZucDA1N3R2M2MyZ2UgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - What does AI have to do with disability, and what is it doing to disability? This question undergirds a roundtable discussion featuring Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes. In brief individual presentations, followed by a moderated discussion, these three experts in the field will tackle the question of AI and disability from a range of distinct and overlapping perspectives. Professor Nagy will examine the remaking of psychiatric disability in an AI era through the case of algorithmic depression diagnostics. Tracing a deep history of attempts to bring computing to bear on depression, he argues that the shift from clinic to program and platform, and the substitution of machine learning features for diagnostic criteria, are rewiring the political economy of diagnosis and overwriting disability identities. Through close reading of contemporary systems and the datasets they depend on, he reveals an emergent technopolitics of disability in action, one that operates at cross-purposes with disability community and activism. Professor Renée Cummings wil discuss what happens when automated systems become gatekeepers of opportunity for individuals with disabilities. Focusing on the data infrastructures governing healthcare, education, employment and public services, she exposes how incomplete datasets, inaccessible design, and reductive classifications can convert ableism into computational logic. Through the lens of data justice, she will confront the ethics of algorithmic exclusion: whose needs are recognized, whose experiences are misread, and who is excluded altogether. Centering accessibility, disability justice, and community expertise, Professor Cummings argues that disabled people must possess meaningful power to design, govern, challenge and—when necessary—refuse the systems shaping their lives. Finally, Dr. Keyes will ask what the history of computational psychiatry teaches us about the political economy of diagnostics.The role of AI in psychiatry is often framed as novel, and focused on improving efficiency and patient access to care. But neither is the case. AI has a long history in the upper echelons of psychiatry, as a field and a practice, and that history has consistently been entangled with broader political conflicts over who plays a role in shaping diagnosis and treatment., and under what conditions. Beginning with the start of computational diagnostics in the 1960s, he will trace out the history of how (and why) computational approaches to psychiatry have come in and out of vogue, arguing that the ultimate purpose of these diagnostic tools is to reshape the political economy of diagnosis and disability. About Jeff Nagy Jeff Nagy is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication and Media Studies at York University. He is a historian of computing and AI, currently focused on the intersection of AI development, the behavioral sciences, and disability. He holds a PhD in Communication from Stanford University. With the DISCO Network, he is a co-author of Technoskepticism: Between Possibility and Refusal (Stanford University Press, 2025). His research and writing have appeared in Parapraxis, n+1, New Media and Society, Technology and Culture, and elsewhere. About Renée Cummings Professor Renée Cummings is an internationally recognized AI governance leader, criminologist, public interest technologist, and public sector intelligence futurist whose work is helping shape how governments, institutions, and organizations prepare for the intelligence age. She is widely recognized as one of the leading global voices advancing responsible AI, trustworthy public sector AI, innovation governance, algorithmic accountability, and the governance frameworks required to strengthen public trust, democratic resilience, and institutional integrity. An award-winning AI innovator and internationally sought-after keynote speaker, Professor Cummings serves as Professor of Practice at the University of Virginia School of Data Science, where she teaches future leaders how to excel with AI and deliver AI excellence. She is also a Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director of the AI Equity Lab at the Brookings Institution and serves as Co-Chair of the Global Academic Network at the Centre for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), one of the world's leading organizations dedicated to AI governance, policy, and digital rights. About Os Keyes Dr. Os A. Keyes is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Massachusetts, Lowell. A widely published and award-winning scholar of everything from the history of medicine to critical approaches to Artificial Intelligence, their first book, Trans Science, is under contract with University of Washington Press. About History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series The History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series brings to campus leading humanities scholars working on issues of media transition and technological emergence. The series promotes new, interdisciplinary approaches to questions about the uses, meanings, causes, and effects of rapid or dramatic shifts in techno-infrastructure, information management, and forms of mediated expression. Presented by BCNM, these events are free and open to the public.

references.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold"
references.description: Abstract: We study how a frontier AI model affects scientific discovery by examining the release of the AlphaFold2 algorithm and its impact on structural biology and related fields of science. Structural biology is the field of science concerned with understanding the structure of proteins. Researchers in this field historically devoted substantial time and resources to experimentally solving three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold can predict these structures without running experiments. In July 2021, researchers gained access to hundreds of thousands of these AI-predicted structures virtually overnight. Yet, to date, we find that the rate of experimental structure determination has remained almost unchanged. Instead, researchers appear to use predicted structures to facilitate and complement experimental structure determination. Looking at downstream science that builds on protein structures, we find that basic research on proteins that had no structural information prior to AlphaFold increases by 23 to 32% relative to proteins that already had a structure, with the effects increasing dramatically over time. This represents a significant shift in the direction of research toward less-studied proteins. By contrast, the response of applied R&D, as measured by patents referencing those proteins, has been far more muted.

references.title: Experiments in Art and Geography
references.description: In this lecture, Trevor Paglen presents a framework for thinking about what happens when artistic practice and geographic method are fused together. Drawing on his work on mass surveillance, computer vision and AI, psyops, and neuroscience, Paglen will discuss art-making not simply as a means of representing geographic research, but as a geographic research method in its own right. Artistic practice can function as a form of fieldwork: a way of investigating landscapes, infrastructures, technologies, and institutions while developing new forms through which to understand them. Paglen will explore how this hybrid practice creates opportunities for collaboration across disciplines and produces forms of knowledge that do not fit neatly within conventional academic or artistic categories. The talk argues that occupying a position neither fully within art nor geography can generate questions, methods, objects, and ways of seeing that neither discipline could produce on its own. Trevor Paglen is a multidisciplinary artist whose practice explores technology, infrastructure, and perception across exhibitions, publications, and public projects worldwide. A MacArthur Fellow and 2026 LG Guggenheim Award winner, he holds advanced degrees from UC Berkeley and the Art Institute of Chicago.

references.title: PMB Seminar with Gautam Dantas | Understanding, Predicting, and Remediating Perturbations to Host-Microbe Interactions
references.description: Antibiotics can acutely and persistently compromise microbiome stability and resilience, enabling enhanced colonization of pathogenic microbes, and loss of host-beneficial functions from depleted commensals. We interrogate resistome, taxonomic, and functional dynamics of microbiota of humans, animals, soils, and built-environments via high-throughput functional metagenomic selections, whole metagenome and transcriptome sequencing, and isolate phenotyping and whole genome sequencing. We use these datasets to model and predict the impact of various biotic and abiotic perturbations on the transmission and evolutionary dynamics of diverse microbiomes and their resistomes across time and habitats, through application of generalized linear mixed models and machine learning algorithms. By integrating community-level analyses of microbiome perturbation and response, with mechanistic analyses of novel microbial resilience functions, we are improving the accuracy and sensitivity of genomics-based methods for diagnosing and treating pathogens and their resistance properties in the clinic and maintaining or rescuing healthy microbiome states.

references.title: All that is compute transforms into concrete: Monopoly rent and the fixity of AI's infrastructure
references.description: In the capitalist imaginary, artificial intelligence is narrated on dematerialization. In this telling, capital has escaped the weight of human labor via the frictionless circulation of data. This paper argues the opposite: the AI economy is a geography of fixity, where training large language models requires warehouse-scale data centers anchored to specific territories by the demands of energy, infrastructure, and available land. Two analytical categories theorize this fixity. The first concerns the monopoly control of location and network proximity: value is extracted from whoever sits closest to the data, controls the interconnection, and commands the lowest latency. The second concerns the monopoly control of computation itself: training frontier AI models is capital-intensive, technically scarce, and concentrated in a handful of firms who can extract a tribute that is not reducible to productivity but to infra/structural position. Both forms of extraction are rent. And both are responses to a profitability crisis in the AI sector driven by rising fixed capital requirements that outpace returns. We draw on financial filings, industry reports, and field observations in Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley to show that what appears as an agglomeration economy is better understood as rent extracted through the strategic fixity of capital in digital infrastructure. Dillon Mahmoudi (dillonm@umbc.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography and Environmental Systems at the University of Maryland Baltimore County. and Alan Wiig (alanwiig@ufl.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography at the University of Florida. They recently published a book chapter, Land for AI: Data Center Real Estate Markets in The Inner World of Artificial Intelligence (2026).

references.title: Rhiju Das: "De novo design of RNA with deep learning"
references.description: RNA design has long been limited by the accuracy of RNA structure prediction. I will describe how the video game Eterna has elicited modeling and design tools for previously intractable pseudoknotted folds, multi-state sensors for disease states, and polymerase ribozymes that copy RNA. AI teams now work alongside Eterna players, and both are scored by prospective high-throughput experiments. Under that pressure, RNA design is improving quickly.
